scenes.narration: Tesla is worth about one point five trillion dollars. That's three hundred and seventy-nine dollars and seventy-eight cents a share at the close on November tenth, twenty twenty-six, times about three point nine five billion shares. And over the last twelve months, it earned about three point two billion dollars. By our math, that's about four hundred and sixty-six times its profit.

And here's the twist. About about thirty-four percent of Tesla's operating profit over those twelve months came from regulatory credits, sold to other carmakers that need them. Not from building cars. So the price is clearly not about today's profit.
So what is this price actually betting on? What has to happen for it to make sense? And what could break the story?
In the next few minutes, we open the machine, follow the cash, run the numbers on what's priced in, and finish with the three numbers to watch when Tesla reports next.
Quick note. This isn't financial advice. Everything here comes from Tesla's own filings and our own math, dated, so you can decide for yourself.

scenes.narration: In twenty twenty-five, Tesla brought in about ninety-five billion dollars. Car sales were about sixty-six billion dollars, down from about seventy-eight and a half billion dollars two years earlier. Deliveries fell too, to about one point six four million. Over the last twelve months, they recovered to about one point seven four million, and two models, the Model Three and the Model Y, were about ninety-eight percent of deliveries last quarter.

Then there are the credits. Over the last twelve months they brought in about one point two billion dollars, almost pure profit. But that's shrinking. Last quarter Tesla reversed four hundred and seventy-five million dollars of credit revenue, and it says new government actions have restricted some credit programs.

The quiet engine is energy. Batteries for homes and power grids brought in about thirteen billion dollars last year, up from about six billion dollars in twenty twenty-three, at a gross margin of about thirty percent. That's a better margin than the cars.

Where are the customers? Over the last twelve months, the United States brought in about forty-six percent of revenue, China about twenty percent, and everywhere else about thirty-four percent. And the map is moving. Last quarter, U S revenue fell fourteen percent, while other international markets grew thirty-two percent. Software is creeping in too. Active Full Self Driving subscriptions reached one point seven four million, up from one point oh four million a year earlier. And services, from repairs to charging, now bring in about sixteen billion dollars a year.

Let me draw the machine. Here are the cars, the big engine with thin margins. Here is energy, smaller but more profitable. Here are the credits, shrinking. And this arrow is the one the price is really about, the future businesses Tesla talks about, that don't have revenue numbers yet.

scenes.narration: So how much cash does all of that actually throw off?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Over the last twelve months, operating cash flow was about eighteen point seven billion dollars. Capex took about fifteen point four billion dollars. Free cash flow was about three point three billion dollars. Operating profit was about three and a half billion dollars, an operating margin of about three percent on about one hundred and four billion dollars of revenue.

And the spending is going up. Tesla expects capex in excess of twenty billion dollars this year, for what it calls super intelligence, meaning computing infrastructure and data centers. It warns that heavy capex will need funding beyond its operating cash. It signed thirty billion dollars of new credit lines, but says it doesn't plan to draw on them this year.

There's a catch in the share count too. Since January of last year, shares outstanding rose about twenty-three percent, almost all from the C E O's pay awards, many of them not yet earned. Count only diluted shares and the value is closer to about one point three five trillion dollars.

On the plus side, the balance sheet is strong. Tesla holds about forty-five billion dollars in cash and short-term investments, against about about nine and a half billion dollars of debt. It pays no dividend and buys back no stock.

Tesla also owns a piece of the Musk universe. In March it put two billion dollars into what is now SpaceX stock. By the end of September that stake was marked at about two point nine billion dollars, and the lock up after the SpaceX listing ends in December. The flow goes both ways. SpaceX bought about six hundred and twenty-six million dollars of Tesla's Megapack batteries this year. These marks move the profit line. Last quarter, net income included a loss of about one hundred and forty million dollars on SpaceX and a gain of about two hundred and ninety million dollars on bitcoin. Meanwhile, capex in the first nine months more than doubled, to about thirteen billion dollars from about six billion dollars.

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the big question. At one and a half trillion dollars, what are you paying for?

scenes.narration: Three quick lenses first, all our math on the last twelve months. Price to earnings, about four hundred and sixty-six times. Free cash flow yield, about zero point two percent. Price to sales, fourteen and a half times. For a car company, all three are far outside the normal range.

Our usual reverse math breaks here, and we want to show you why. To justify the price from today's free cash flow, that cash would need to grow about forty-five percent a year with an eight percent discount rate, or about fifty-two percent at ten, every year for a decade. At a yield this small, tiny changes swing the answer, so it isn't a useful number.

So here's a simpler lens, our rough illustration. For the price to work as a steady business growing three percent a year from here, Tesla would need free cash flow of about about seventy-three billion dollars to about one hundred and two billion dollars a year. That's twenty-two to thirty-one times today, or seventy percent to ninety-eight percent of today's entire revenue.

In other words, the price is not about cars at today's margins. It's a bet on businesses that barely show up in the numbers yet. Robotaxis, the self-driving software, energy storage and robots. Even the C E O's pay package starts paying out only above two trillion dollars of market value, and today's value is below that first milestone. Those are pay terms, not forecasts.

scenes.narration: Number one, autonomy becomes revenue. Tesla says it started Robotaxi rides with Cybercabs in Austin in September, and that its fleet passed nearly two million unsupervised miles. Active self-driving subscriptions reached one point seven four million, up from one point zero four million a year earlier. Tesla doesn't report Robotaxi revenue yet.

Number two, energy keeps growing at about a thirty percent margin. Tesla says its battery business has its highest ever order rate and backlog, and a new Texas factory started production with planned capacity of fifty gigawatt hours.

Number three, the robots become a product. Tesla says Optimus production began on high volume lines in Fremont. There are no revenue figures. One of the pay package milestones is a million robots delivered.

And number four, the car business recovers without the credits. Deliveries went from about one point seven nine million in twenty twenty-four to about one point six four million last year. Tesla says batteries are now the limit on car volumes, and that its order backlog for cars is the largest in four years. Margins have to hold as the credits fade, because the price can't lean on them anymore.

scenes.narration: Risk one is one person. Tesla's own filing says it is highly dependent on Elon Musk, who doesn't devote his full time to Tesla and also runs other companies. It warns that if he pledged shares for loans, he might be forced to sell. And it says the pay package could pull focus toward specific technologies.

scenes.narration: Risk two is demand and policy. Growth depends on people buying electric cars and adopting self-driving. Competition keeps growing. Tax credits have been repealed or restricted, and tariffs hit the energy business harder than the cars.

And the margin is already thin. Over the last twelve months, Tesla's operating margin was three point three percent. Operating expenses last quarter were about four point eight billion dollars, up from about three point four billion dollars a year earlier, which Tesla puts down to its super intelligence and other research projects, and to stock pay, including the C E O's award. A securities class action over its Autopilot, self driving and Robotaxi claims is also pending. So the costs of the bet arrive before the revenue does.

Risk three is the courts and regulators. In one Autopilot case, a jury awarded a hundred and twenty-nine million dollars in damages, plus two hundred million dollars in punitive damages, and Tesla is appealing. Regulators are asking about driver assistance and Robotaxi. No agency has found wrongdoing, and no amounts are disclosed.

And the upside the price might not fully include. Tesla says the Semi is in volume production, Cybercab capacity is over a hundred and twenty-five thousand a year, and its self-driving software is now offered in nine E U countries. It also owns a stake in SpaceX, which went public this year. None of it comes with a revenue figure, so we won't put one on it.

scenes.narration: So, what should you watch?

Here's the scorecard for the next report, expected in late January twenty twenty-seven, our estimate. One, fourth quarter deliveries, against four hundred and eighteen thousand a year earlier. Two, capex and free cash flow, as spending passes twenty billion. Three, regulatory credits and the car margin without them. If those hold up, the story the price is telling keeps holding up. If they crack, the bet on the future gets much harder to defend.
That's Tesla, November twenty twenty-six edition. We'll update it after every report, with new numbers and the same three questions. What's priced in, what has to happen, and what could go wrong.
